display_name: Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera, Barolo
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "A Barolo that channels the Langhe’s soil split — Tortonian calcareous marls to the west and Helvetian sandstones to the east — into classic Nebbiolo aromatics: rose, tar and iron-tinged tannins. Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera is an appellation-level bottling that has repeatedly earned international tasting medals, signaling consistent, export-ready style.",
  "wine_summary": "Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera is a Barolo made from 100% Nebbiolo under the strict aging rules of the appellation, so expect the structural signature of Barolo: high acidity, firm, fine-grained tannins, and aromatic notes of rose petal, tar and dried cherry. The producer's repeated success at competitions (multiple Berliner Wine Trophy golds and an Asia Wine Trophy gold) points to reliable pick, extraction and maturation practices geared to a classic Barolo profile rather than a flamboyant, modernist take. Terroir matters here because Barolo’s communes range from younger, calcareous Sant'Agata Fossili marls in the west — which lift fragrance and early approachability — to older Lequio Formation marls and Helvetian sandstones in the east — which add iron and structural rigidity; an appellation-level blend will typically aim to balance those poles.",
  "terroir_expression": "Barolo’s soil divide directly shapes what you taste: wines influenced by Tortonian calcareous marls (Sant'Agata Fossili) show brighter red fruit and lifted floral perfume, while parcels on Helvetian sandstone and compacted Lequio marl contribute dense tannin, darker fruit and a metallic/iron note. An appellation Barolo like this one tastes the way it does because Nebbiolo translates those geological differences into perfume versus grip — the mix of calcium-rich marl and iron-laden sandstone produces floral aromatics up front and a drying, mineral-backed finish.",
  "vinification_summary": "Specific public details about Terre del Barolo’s exact vinification choices for the Arnaldo Rivera bottling are limited, but the wine follows Barolo’s legal framework of extended aging (minimum 18 months in wood, total minimum 38 months), which implies prolonged maceration and maturation that extract Nebbiolo’s tannins and tertiary aromas. In practice, longer maceration and the use of large neutral casks (botti) versus small new barrique change texture: large casks preserve Nebbiolo’s verticality and fine tannin grain, while small new oak would add vanilla and rounder tannins — this bottle’s medal-winning, classically aromatic profile suggests a restrained oak approach.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Braised beef cheek with polenta — the rich collagen and earthy jus soften Barolo’s tannins while the polenta mirrors the wine’s mineral starchiness.",
    "Tajarin al ragù (hand-cut egg pasta with slow-cooked beef ragù) — the wine’s acidity cuts the fattiness and its rose-tar aromatics lift the herb and tomato notes.",
    "Mature pecorino and thinly sliced prosciutto crudo — salt and fat tame tannin and let the wine’s dried cherry and cedar notes sing; a casual but precise snack pairing.",
    "Venison osso buco with gremolata — gamey meat and the herbaceous gremolata highlight Nebbiolo’s leather and dried herb facets, and the wine stands up to intense flavors in a fine-dining setting."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": "Fontanafredda Barolo — comparable as an appellation-level Barolo that blends communes to balance perfume and structure; similar price bracket and approach. Marchesi di Barolo Barolo — another village-to-appellation expression that favors traditional aging and delivers firm Nebbiolo tannins and classic aromatics.",
  "style_profile": "Nebbiolo-based medium-bodied red with high acidity, very firm tannins, and floral-tar minerality",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drinkable now from decanting for younger vintages, but best cellared; store at 12–14°C on its side. Expect primary perfume to evolve into truffle, leather and dried flowers over a decade-plus.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: $40–$60 retail. Competes with Fontanafredda Barolo and Marchesi di Barolo’s entry Barolos in this band. It is worth buying if you want a reliably classic, medal-winning Barolo that trades single-vineyard prestige for consistent, ageworthy structure.",
  "market_position": "Collectors who want accessible Barolos for short- to mid-term cellaring and restaurants building classic Italian lists are the primary audience. The bottle performs well in retail as an approachable Barolo offering recognizable Nebbiolo traits for consumers stepping up from Chianti or Barbera.",
  "insider_take": "This is the Barolo to buy when you want textbook Nebbiolo tannin and rose-tar aromatics without paying cru prices; the tradeoff is vineyard specificity — if you want a single-vineyard, site-specific Barolo with a pronounced sense of place, look to La Morra or Serralunga single-MGA bottles instead. parsed.terroir_expression: Barolo’s soil divide directly shapes what you taste: wines influenced by Tortonian calcareous marls (Sant'Agata Fossili) show brighter red fruit and lifted floral perfume, while parcels on Helvetian sandstone and compacted Lequio marl contribute dense tannin, darker fruit and a metallic/iron note. An appellation Barolo like this one tastes the way it does because Nebbiolo translates those geological differences into perfume versus grip — the mix of calcium-rich marl and iron-laden sandstone produces floral aromatics up front and a drying, mineral-backed finish.
parsed.vinification_summary: Specific public details about Terre del Barolo’s exact vinification choices for the Arnaldo Rivera bottling are limited, but the wine follows Barolo’s legal framework of extended aging (minimum 18 months in wood, total minimum 38 months), which implies prolonged maceration and maturation that extract Nebbiolo’s tannins and tertiary aromas. In practice, longer maceration and the use of large neutral casks (botti) versus small new barrique change texture: large casks preserve Nebbiolo’s verticality and fine tannin grain, while small new oak would add vanilla and rounder tannins — this bottle’s medal-winning, classically aromatic profile suggests a restrained oak approach.
food_pairing: Braised beef cheek with polenta — the rich collagen and earthy jus soften Barolo’s tannins while the polenta mirrors the wine’s mineral starchiness.
Tajarin al ragù (hand-cut egg pasta with slow-cooked beef ragù) — the wine’s acidity cuts the fattiness and its rose-tar aromatics lift the herb and tomato notes.
Mature pecorino and thinly sliced prosciutto crudo — salt and fat tame tannin and let the wine’s dried cherry and cedar notes sing; a casual but precise snack pairing.
Venison osso buco with gremolata — gamey meat and the herbaceous gremolata highlight Nebbiolo’s leather and dried herb facets, and the wine stands up to intense flavors in a fine-dining setting.

parsed.market_position: Collectors who want accessible Barolos for short- to mid-term cellaring and restaurants building classic Italian lists are the primary audience. The bottle performs well in retail as an approachable Barolo offering recognizable Nebbiolo traits for consumers stepping up from Chianti or Barbera.
parsed.insider_take: This is the Barolo to buy when you want textbook Nebbiolo tannin and rose-tar aromatics without paying cru prices; the tradeoff is vineyard specificity — if you want a single-vineyard, site-specific Barolo with a pronounced sense of place, look to La Morra or Serralunga single-MGA bottles instead. For dinner service and early drinking with decanting, this will perform better and cost less than many named-cru alternatives.
